best_practices: Always choose HTML elements based on their semantic meaning and document hierarchy, never merely for their default browser styling.
Adopt a mobile-first responsive approach: establish robust baseline styling for small screens before enhancing with min-width media queries.
Use CSS custom properties for colors, spacing, and typography to maintain a cohesive, maintainable design token system.
Rely on Flexbox for one-dimensional component alignment and CSS Grid for two-dimensional page layouts; avoid legacy float-based page structures.
Ensure interactive elements are accessible: maintain visible focus indicators, preserve logical tab order, and test with the keyboard alone.
Optimize images for the web: provide explicit width and height attributes, use modern formats, and apply lazy loading only to below-the-fold media.
Maintain clean, organized source repositories with meaningful file naming, relative asset paths, and clear README documentation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Overusing generic <div> elements ('div soup') instead of semantic landmarks (<header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <footer>).
common_mistakes.why_it_happens: Beginners focus purely on visual layout rather than document meaning and accessibility.
common_mistakes.professional_approach: Structure documents using semantic HTML landmarks to ensure search engines and assistive technologies understand page structure.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using fixed pixel widths (e.g., width: 1200px) that cause horizontal scrolling and layout breakage on mobile devices.
common_mistakes.why_it_happens: Designing exclusively for desktop screens without testing responsive viewport resizing.
common_mistakes.professional_approach: Use fluid widths (percentages, max-width: 100%, relative units rem/em) and mobile-first media queries to accommodate all screen sizes.

common_mistakes.mistake: Removing focus outlines with outline: none without providing an accessible visible replacement.
common_mistakes.why_it_happens: Viewing default browser focus outlines as visually intrusive without understanding keyboard navigation needs.
common_mistakes.professional_approach: Style custom, high-contrast focus rings using :focus-visible so keyboard users can easily track their active position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming static HTML forms store and email submitted data automatically without a configured backend or service.
common_mistakes.why_it_happens: Confusing the client-side form interface and browser validation with server-side processing.
common_mistakes.professional_approach: Clearly recognize the boundary: HTML forms collect and validate input in the browser, but submitting and storing data requires an external handler.

common_mistakes.mistake: Blindly pasting AI-generated CSS without understanding cascade specificity or testing intermediate screen widths.
common_mistakes.why_it_happens: Relying on AI output as a finished solution without verifying cross-browser behavior.
common_mistakes.professional_approach: Read every line of generated code, inspect computed styles in DevTools, test responsive widths, and refine manually.

lessons.expected_outcome: Ability to explain how a browser retrieves and displays a static HTML web page from a web server.

File naming standards: lowercase, hyphen-separated filenames without spaces
Understanding relative paths (./, ../) vs absolute URLs
HTML document template: <!DOCTYPE html>, <html>, <head>, and <body>
Essential metadata: <meta charset="UTF-8">, <meta name="viewport">, and descriptive <title> tags

lessons.what_learner_does: Creates a structured project directory in VS Code and writes their first boilerplate HTML5 document from scratch.

Paragraphs (

Semantic text tags: <strong> for importance, <em> for emphasis, <mark>, <small>, <code>
Unordered (<ul>) and ordered (<ol>) lists for structured grouped content
Anchor links (<a>): href attributes, relative page links, external links with rel="noopener noreferrer", and in-page anchor IDs

lessons.lesson_title: Media Assets, Tabular Data & Semantic Landmarks

Writing informative alt text for content images vs empty alt="" for purely decorative graphics
Editorial images with captions using <figure> and <figcaption>
Tabular data structure: <table>, <thead>, <tbody>, <tr>, <th> with scope attribute, and <td>
HTML5 landmark elements: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <aside>, and <footer>
Evaluating semantic tags vs generic <div> containers to avoid 'div soup'
lessons.why_it_matters: Appropriate semantic landmarks establish meaningful screen-reader regions and improve technical SEO ranking without extra styling code.

lessons.lesson_title: Native HTML Forms, Input Validation & Quality QA
lessons.what_is_taught: Form architecture (<form>), form controls (<input>, <textarea>, <select>, <button>), explicit label associations, native browser validation, and W3C validation.

Pairing form labels explicitly using the for and id attributes for accessibility

Multi-line input (<textarea>), dropdown options (<select> and <option>), and submit buttons
Native validation attributes: required, minlength, maxlength, min, max, and pattern
HTML comments, code indentation standards, and testing markup with the W3C Markup Validation Service
lessons.why_it_matters: Accessible form markup with native validation provides immediate user feedback and allows assistive technologies to announce required inputs correctly.

lessons.expected_outcome: A fully functional, native-validated HTML form interface that passes W3C validation with zero structural errors.

modules.title: Professional CSS Fundamentals
modules.objective: Teach students to style web interfaces professionally while mastering the CSS cascade, layout box model, typography hierarchy, and reusable design token architectures.
modules.module_purpose: Master CSS selectors, cascade resolution, specificity, box model mechanics, positioning, typography, colors, custom properties, and DevTools inspection.
what_you_will_learn: Connect external stylesheets and write clean, maintainable CSS syntax adhering to industry conventions.
Master CSS selector types: element, class, ID, attribute, combinators, pseudo-classes, and pseudo-elements.
Understand the CSS cascade, specificity calculations, source order, inheritance, and why to avoid !important.
Apply the CSS box model, understand box-sizing: border-box, dimension constraints, margin collapsing, and overflow handling.
Utilize CSS positioning (static, relative, absolute, fixed, sticky) and manage stacking contexts with z-index.
Establish professional typography systems with web-safe and hosted fonts, font scale ratios, and readable line lengths.
Architect reusable design tokens using CSS custom properties (:root variables) for colors, spacing, and border radii.
Inspect and debug CSS properties, computed values, and box models in real time using Chrome DevTools.

lessons.lesson_title: CSS Syntax, Selectors & Cascade Architecture
lessons.what_is_taught: Linking external stylesheets, CSS rule anatomy, basic and advanced selectors, pseudo-classes, pseudo-elements, the cascade, specificity, and inheritance.
subtopics: Linking stylesheets via <link rel="stylesheet"> vs inline styles and <style> tags
Selectors: type, class (.), ID (#), attribute ([type="..."]), child (>), and descendant combinators
Pseudo-classes (:hover, :focus, :active, :first-child, :nth-child) and pseudo-elements (::before, ::after)
The Cascade: Origin, Specificity calculation (Inline, ID, Class, Type), and Source Order
Inherited CSS properties vs non-inherited properties, and the hazards of relying on !important
CSS normalization and universal resetting (* { box-sizing: border-box; margin: 0; padding: 0; })
lessons.why_it_matters: Mastering the cascade and specificity eliminates frustrating styling conflicts and prevents developers from cluttering stylesheets with hacky overrides.
lessons.what_learner_does: Calculates specificity scores for complex selectors and reorganizes a messy stylesheet to eliminate all !important declarations.
lessons.expected_outcome: A clean, predictable stylesheet architecture where selectors target elements with minimal, balanced specificity.

lessons.lesson_title: The CSS Box Model, Dimensions & Overflow
lessons.what_is_taught: The CSS box model layers, content-box vs border-box, width, height, min/max dimensions, margin collapsing, display modes, and overflow handling.
subtopics: Box model layers: content area, padding, border, and margin
Why universal box-sizing: border-box simplifies responsive layout math
Width and height sizing: explicit dimensions, min-width, max-width, min-height, and max-height
Understanding display properties: block, inline, inline-block, and none
Vertical margin collapsing mechanics and how to prevent unintended spacing gaps
Controlling container overflow: visible, hidden, scroll, and auto, and diagnosing unintended scrollbars
lessons.why_it_matters: The box model governs how every single HTML element is sized and spaced on a web page; misunderstanding it causes broken layouts.
lessons.what_learner_does: Builds a series of card containers with exact padding, border, and margin values, inspecting their box models in DevTools.
lessons.expected_outcome: Ability to accurately predict and control element dimensions and eliminate accidental layout overflows.

lessons.lesson_title: CSS Positioning, Coordinates & Stacking Contexts
lessons.what_is_taught: Normal flow vs positioned layout, static, relative, absolute, fixed, and sticky positioning, offset coordinates, z-index, and stacking contexts.
subtopics: Normal document flow and when out-of-flow positioning is genuinely required
position: relative: self-offsetting and establishing positioning contexts for child elements
position: absolute: anchoring elements relative to the nearest positioned ancestor
position: fixed: creating sticky top navigation bars and persistent notification banners
position: sticky: combining relative and fixed behaviors based on scroll thresholds
Understanding z-index layering and diagnosing stacking context traps
lessons.why_it_matters: Positioning allows precise placement of badges, sticky navigation, and modal overlays, but misuse can detach elements from natural responsive flow.
lessons.what_learner_does: Builds a sticky website header and a card component featuring an absolutely positioned promotional badge.
lessons.expected_outcome: Mastery over CSS positioning mechanics without breaking normal document responsiveness.

lessons.lesson_title: Typography Systems, Color Models & Visual Depth
lessons.what_is_taught: Web typography, hosted fonts (Google Fonts), font-display, font scales, line-height, letter-spacing, HEX/RGB/HSL color models, borders, border-radius, and shadows.
subtopics: Font families: serif, sans-serif, monospace, and system font fallback stacks
Importing and optimizing Google Fonts with preconnect and font-display: swap
Establishing a modular typography scale: font-size, font-weight, line-height (1.4–1.6), and letter-spacing
Enforcing readable body text line lengths (45 to 75 characters per line using max-width: 65ch)
Color models: HEX (#004672), RGB/RGBA, and HSL/HSLA for intuitive color adjustments
Visual depth: borders, border-radius curves, subtle box-shadow elevation systems, and background gradients
lessons.why_it_matters: Clean typography and harmonious color contrast define whether a website looks amateurish or polished and authoritative.
lessons.what_learner_does: Styles a typography specimen sheet featuring balanced heading and body type scales, contrast-verified colors, and elevation cards.
lessons.expected_outcome: A sophisticated typographic rhythm and cohesive visual styling applied across all core HTML elements.

lessons.lesson_title: CSS Custom Properties, Design Tokens & DevTools QA
lessons.what_is_taught: CSS variables (:root), primitive vs semantic design tokens, mathematical functions (calc(), clamp(), min(), max()), and Chrome DevTools debugging.
subtopics: Declaring and consuming CSS custom properties (--color-brand, var(--color-brand))
Primitive design values vs semantic tokens (--color-primary vs --color-text-body)
Establishing consistent design token scales for colors, spacing (8px rhythm), radii, and font sizes
CSS math functions: calc() for dynamic offsets, clamp() for fluid sizing, min() and max()
Chrome DevTools Styles panel: inspecting computed properties, toggling declarations, and editing values live
Debugging selector matching, overridden properties, and box model visualizers in DevTools
lessons.why_it_matters: Custom properties enable rapid site-wide theme adjustments, maintainable codebases, and seamless design token synchronization.
lessons.what_learner_does: Refactors an entire stylesheet to use a comprehensive design token architecture defined in the :root selector.
lessons.expected_outcome: A production-grade, token-driven stylesheet where colors, spacing, and typography update globally from single variable definitions.

modules.title: Modern Responsive Layouts
modules.objective: Teach students to build fluid, responsive websites that adapt seamlessly across mobile, tablet, desktop, and intermediate screen widths using modern CSS Flexbox, Grid, and container queries.
modules.module_purpose: THIS IS THE CORE TECHNICAL MODULE. Master mobile-first design, fluid relative units, CSS Flexbox (1D), CSS Grid (2D), media queries, container queries, responsive images, and viewport stress testing.
what_you_will_learn: Adopt a strict mobile-first responsive design methodology using fluid relative units (rem, em, %, vw, vh, clamp()).
Master CSS Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts: flex directions, axis alignments, wrapping, gaps, and flexible item sizing.
Master CSS Grid for two-dimensional layouts: explicit/implicit tracks, fractional fr units, repeat(), minmax(), and auto-fit/auto-fill.
Implement mobile-first media queries targeting content-driven breakpoints rather than arbitrary device widths.
Implement modern CSS container queries (@container) to create self-responsive components that adapt to their container width.
Deliver responsive images using max-width: 100%, object-fit, srcset, sizes, and <picture> elements.
Test and debug layouts across 5 representative viewports (320px, 390px, 768px, 1024px, 1440px) ensuring zero horizontal scrollbar bugs.

lessons.lesson_title: Responsive Principles, Mobile-First & Relative Units
lessons.what_is_taught: Responsive web design foundations, viewport meta tag, mobile-first vs desktop-first philosophy, relative sizing units (rem, em, %, vw, vh, dvh), and fluid clamp() typography.
subtopics: Why fixed-pixel desktop layouts fail on modern multi-screen devices
The viewport meta tag and its role in preventing mobile browser zoom emulation
Mobile-first development: establishing small-screen baseline CSS and progressively enhancing with min-width queries
Relative units: why rem is preferred for typography and spacing, em for component-relative scaling, and % for fluid widths
Modern viewport units: vw, vh, vmin, vmax, and dynamic dvh/svh to handle mobile browser address bars
Fluid typography and spacing formulas using clamp(min, preferred, max)
lessons.why_it_matters: Mobile-first development ensures smaller mobile devices download only necessary styles and render fast, clean interfaces.
lessons.what_learner_does: Calculates and implements fluid typography and spacing scales that scale smoothly between 320px and 1440px without abrupt jumps.
lessons.expected_outcome: A fluid layout foundation where font sizes and container padding scale proportionally across all viewport widths.

lessons.lesson_title: CSS Flexbox: One-Dimensional Layout Architecture
lessons.what_is_taught: Flexbox layout engine, main and cross axes, flex container properties, item alignment, multi-line wrapping, gap spacing, and flexible item sizing.
subtopics: Initializing flex containers: display: flex and display: inline-flex
Understanding main axis vs cross axis orientation with flex-direction (row, column, row-reverse, column-reverse)
Aligning items along the main axis using justify-content (flex-start, center, space-between, space-around, space-evenly)
Aligning items along the cross axis using align-items and per-item align-self overrides
Enabling multi-line wrapping with flex-wrap: wrap and spacing items using gap, row-gap, and column-gap
Controlling item growth and shrinkage: flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis, and the flex shorthand
Building responsive navigation bars, centered hero callouts, and aligned button rows
lessons.why_it_matters: Flexbox is the definitive modern standard for 1D component layouts, replacing fragile floats and inline-block hacks.
lessons.what_learner_does: Builds a flexible header with logo and navigation links that reflows gracefully from a horizontal bar to a stacked mobile menu.
lessons.expected_outcome: A perfectly aligned, responsive navigation header and button group built entirely with Flexbox.

lessons.lesson_title: CSS Grid: Two-Dimensional Page Layouts
lessons.what_is_taught: CSS Grid architecture, grid tracks, columns, rows, fractional fr units, repeat(), minmax(), auto-fit, auto-fill, grid gaps, and explicit item placement.
subtopics: Initializing grid containers: display: grid and grid-template-columns / grid-template-rows
The fractional unit (fr) and how it distributes available free space proportionally
Dynamic track generation using repeat() and flexible sizing bounds with minmax(min, max)
Building auto-responsive card grids without media queries using repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr))
Spacing grid cells cleanly using the modern gap property
Explicit item placement across grid lines using grid-column and grid-row spanning
Knowing when to use Flexbox (1D content flow) versus CSS Grid (2D structured page layouts)
lessons.why_it_matters: CSS Grid provides native two-dimensional layout power that makes complex card galleries and multi-column web pages trivial to build.
lessons.what_learner_does: Constructs an auto-responsive product/service card gallery that automatically reflows from 1 column on mobile to 4 columns on widescreen.
lessons.expected_outcome: A responsive, two-dimensional card grid that adapts dynamically to viewport width without requiring multiple media queries.

lessons.lesson_title: Media Queries, Breakpoints & Content Adaptation
lessons.what_is_taught: Media query syntax, mobile-first min-width query structures, content-driven breakpoint selection, avoiding device-specific traps, and layout reflow.
subtopics: Media query syntax: @media (min-width: 48em) and @media (min-width: 64em) using relative units
Mobile-first breakpoint progression: base (mobile) -> min-width: 768px (tablet) -> min-width: 1024px (desktop)
Content-driven breakpoints: introducing a media query when content naturally breaks, not because an iPhone has that width
Restructuring page sections across breakpoints: converting stacked mobile stacks into side-by-side columns
Adapting navigation, header heights, and footer multi-column layouts across tablet and desktop viewports
Diagnosing and eliminating unintended horizontal scrollbars caused by oversized fixed widths
lessons.why_it_matters: Carefully planned media queries ensure content hierarchy remains readable and touch-friendly on small screens while taking advantage of desktop screen real estate.
lessons.what_learner_does: Implements progressive media queries to reflow a multi-section landing page seamlessly across phone, tablet, and desktop viewports.
lessons.expected_outcome: A cohesive responsive layout that reflows smoothly without awkward layout jumps or horizontal overflow.

lessons.lesson_title: CSS Container Queries, Responsive Images & Viewport QA
lessons.what_is_taught: Container queries (@container), container-type: inline-size, container-based card reflow, responsive images (srcset, sizes, <picture>), and 5-viewport DevTools QA.
subtopics: The fundamental limitation of viewport media queries for modular, reusable components
Establishing query containers with container-type: inline-size and optional container-name
Writing container queries: @container (min-width: 35rem) to adapt card layouts based on parent width
Responsive images: fluid max-width: 100%, height: auto, and aspect-ratio to prevent layout shift
Resolution switching with srcset and sizes, and art direction using the <picture> element
Chrome DevTools Device Mode testing protocol across 5 target widths: 320px, 390px, 768px, 1024px, and 1440px
Stress-testing layouts with long strings, German words, and 200% browser zoom
lessons.why_it_matters: Container queries represent the biggest modern leap in CSS, allowing components to adapt to their surrounding space anywhere on a page.
lessons.what_learner_does: Creates a card component that switches from a stacked card to an editorial horizontal card when placed in a wide container, and audits across all 5 test widths.
lessons.expected_outcome: A modern container-query component and verified responsive page that passes stress-testing at 320px, 390px, 768px, 1024px, and 1440px.

modules.title: UI Components & Interactions
modules.objective: Teach students to create reusable, accessible HTML and CSS interface components and lightweight visual micro-interactions with reduced-motion support.
modules.module_purpose: Master component thinking without frameworks, interactive button states, accessible navigation, card patterns, accessible form styling, CSS transitions, keyframes, and prefers-reduced-motion.
what_you_will_learn: Adopt component-driven CSS thinking without requiring complex JavaScript frameworks.
Design accessible button systems distinguishing buttons (<button>) from links (<a>), with hover, focus, active, and disabled states.
Implement accessible navigation and native disclosure accordions using <details> and <summary> without fragile checkbox hacks.
Build versatile card components (services, features, testimonials, pricing) with cohesive spacing and typography.
Style accessible form controls (inputs, textareas, selects, custom checkboxes/radios) with user-invalid feedback states.
Create smooth CSS transitions and subtle keyframe animations using hardware-accelerated transform and opacity properties.
Support user accessibility preferences using the @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) media query.

lessons.lesson_title: Component Thinking, Links vs Buttons & State Architecture
lessons.what_is_taught: Component thinking in vanilla CSS, links (navigation) vs buttons (actions), interactive states (:hover, :focus, :focus-visible, :active, :disabled), and visible focus rings.
subtopics: Component thinking without frameworks: reusable classes, modifiers, and consistent naming
Crucial semantic distinction: <a> navigates to a new URL/anchor; <button> triggers an action or script
Styling all interactive states: default, :hover, :focus-visible (keyboard focus), :active (press), and :disabled
Why outline: none without a custom focus indicator is an accessibility failure
Designing high-contrast custom focus rings with outline, outline-offset, and box-shadow
Building primary, secondary, and outline button component variants
lessons.why_it_matters: Using the wrong element for links or buttons breaks keyboard accessibility, screen-reader announcements, and expected browser behavior.
lessons.what_learner_does: Builds a reusable button component suite and tests all hover and focus states using mouse and keyboard.
lessons.expected_outcome: A modular button library with accessible keyboard focus indicators and tactile interactive states.

lessons.lesson_title: Accessible Navigation & Native Disclosure Accordions
lessons.what_is_taught: Navigation landmark patterns, accessible disclosure elements (<details> and <summary>), styling disclosure triangles, and limitations of CSS-only mobile menus.
subtopics: Semantic navigation structure: <nav aria-label="Main"> and unordered lists <ul><li><a>
Desktop horizontal menus vs mobile wrapping navigation patterns
The limitations of CSS-only hamburger menus and why hidden checkbox hacks are fragile and inaccessible
Native disclosure elements: <details> and <summary> for accessible FAQ accordions and mobile drawers
Styling <details[open]> states and animating disclosures smoothly using modern CSS
Progressive enhancement: understanding when interactive navigation requires JavaScript in production
lessons.why_it_matters: Navigation is the primary way users explore a website; accessible patterns ensure keyboard and screen-reader users can access all sections.
lessons.what_learner_does: Builds an accessible FAQ accordion and a clean responsive navigation bar using semantic landmarks and native <details>.
lessons.expected_outcome: An accessible navigation bar and interactive disclosure accordion that operate seamlessly with keyboard navigation.

lessons.lesson_title: Modern Card Design Patterns & Content Layouts
lessons.what_is_taught: Card anatomy, service cards, feature cards, media cards with responsive imagery, testimonial quote cards, pricing table layouts, and elevation depth.
subtopics: Card anatomy: visual media container, content body, metadata tags, and action buttons
Building service cards with custom icons and concise descriptive copy
Feature cards with hover elevation transitions using box-shadow and transform: translateY(-4px)
Testimonial cards featuring <blockquote>, <cite>, and accessible customer attributions
Pricing card layouts: highlighting featured tiers, displaying billing cadences, and list checks
Ensuring clickable cards remain accessible without wrapping entire cards in invalid massive anchor tags
lessons.why_it_matters: Cards are the most versatile UI component in modern web design, used across portfolios, e-commerce, and service sites.
lessons.what_learner_does: Constructs a coordinated set of 3 card layouts (service, testimonial, and pricing) using shared design tokens.
lessons.expected_outcome: A polished card component collection with consistent padding, typography, hover elevation, and responsive reflow.

lessons.lesson_title: Accessible Form Styling & Native User Feedback
lessons.what_is_taught: Styling form controls, custom focus states, floating labels vs static labels, fieldset/legend grouping, error presentation with :user-invalid, and backend boundaries.
subtopics: Styling text inputs, textareas, and select dropdowns with consistent padding, borders, and typography
Styling custom checkboxes and radio buttons accessibly using hidden native inputs and peer sibling selectors
Grouping related controls with <fieldset> and <legend> (e.g., billing address, service preferences)
Modern validation pseudo-classes: styling error states using :invalid and the modern :user-invalid pseudo-class
Clear commercial transparency: explaining why static HTML forms require an external handler or server to process submissions
Designing clear success and error confirmation layouts for client-side forms
lessons.why_it_matters: Poorly styled or unlabelled forms create high friction, causing users to abandon contact or registration flows.
lessons.what_learner_does: Styles a complete, accessible contact form with custom focus rings and real-time validation error feedback.
lessons.expected_outcome: A professional, accessible form interface that provides clear visual feedback and guides users through required inputs.

lessons.lesson_title: CSS Transitions, Keyframe Animations & Reduced Motion
lessons.what_is_taught: CSS transitions, timing functions, cubic-bezier, transform and opacity optimization, keyframe animations (@keyframes), and prefers-reduced-motion accessibility.
subtopics: CSS transition properties: transition-property, transition-duration, transition-timing-function (ease, linear, ease-in-out)
Performance rule: animating only composite-friendly properties (transform and opacity) to prevent layout thrashing
Keyframe animations: @keyframes rule, animation-name, animation-duration, and animation-iteration-count
Creating subtle micro-interactions: button pulses, fading in elements, and smooth accordion expansions
Vestibular accessibility and motion sickness: understanding user sensitivities to continuous motion
Implementing @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) to disable or soften animations for users who request reduced motion
lessons.why_it_matters: Subtle animations bring interfaces to life, but excessive or non-negotiable motion can cause dizziness and vestibular distress for sensitive users.
lessons.what_learner_does: Adds smooth hover and card entrance animations, and writes a prefers-reduced-motion media query that safely replaces motion with instant fades.
lessons.expected_outcome: A set of performant, delightful UI interactions that respect user motion preferences automatically.

lessons.lesson_title: Web Accessibility Foundations & WCAG 2.2 AA
lessons.what_is_taught: Web accessibility principles, WCAG 2.2 Level AA guidelines, semantic HTML as accessibility's backbone, ARIA First Rule, heading structure, and accessible link text.
subtopics: Why web accessibility is both an ethical imperative and a commercial necessity for digital products
WCAG 2.2 principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust (POUR)
The First Rule of ARIA: use native HTML5 semantic elements rather than adding ARIA roles to <div> elements
Validating document outline: ensuring sequential heading hierarchy without skipped heading levels
Writing meaningful, context-independent link text (eliminating 'click here', 'read more', or naked URLs)
Appropriate alternative text: informative descriptions vs empty alt="" for decorative background elements
lessons.why_it_matters: Accessible websites reach wider audiences, rank higher in search engines, and comply with global digital accessibility standards.
lessons.what_learner_does: Audits a sample web page with missing landmarks, skipped headings, and unlabelled links, refactoring it for WCAG AA compliance.
lessons.expected_outcome: A semantic, accessible document structure that communicates meaning clearly to screen readers and assistive tech.

lessons.lesson_title: Keyboard Operability, Focus Visibility & Color Contrast
lessons.what_is_taught: Manual keyboard testing protocols (Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space), logical tab order, preventing keyboard traps, high-contrast focus indicators, and color contrast calculations.
subtopics: The manual keyboard test: navigating an entire website using only the Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, and Space keys
Ensuring a logical DOM focus order that matches the visual layout flow
Identifying and fixing keyboard traps where focus cannot escape an interactive component
Styling high-contrast visible focus indicators using :focus-visible across all interactive elements
WCAG AA contrast requirements: 4.5:1 for normal text (< 18pt), 3:1 for large text (>= 18pt or 14pt bold)

faq.question: What is HTML, CSS & Responsive Web Design?
faq.answer: HTML, CSS & Responsive Web Design is a practical, beginner-entry certification course that teaches you to build modern, accessible, and fast-loading websites from scratch. You will learn semantic HTML5 to structure web content, modern CSS3 to style interfaces, and responsive layout techniques (Flexbox, CSS Grid, media queries, and container queries) to ensure websites look professional across mobile, tablet, and desktop screens.

faq.question: Is this course suitable for complete beginners?
faq.answer: Yes. The course assumes zero previous programming or web development experience. We start with web fundamentals, how browsers work, and basic HTML before advancing systematically into CSS styling, responsive layouts, accessibility, and real website publishing.

faq.question: What is the duration and fee?
faq.answer: The course duration is 6 Weeks, comprising 48 intensive learning hours (8 hours per week across guided software labs and hands-on coding exercises). The flat tuition fee is ₹6,900 with transparent pricing and no hidden costs or artificial comparison markups.

faq.question: Do I need any previous coding experience?
faq.answer: No prior coding or programming experience is required. All you need is basic computer literacy (managing files and folders, using a web browser, and basic typing). We teach all code from the ground up.

faq.question: Will I learn HTML5 and modern CSS?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn modern HTML5 standards (semantic tags, landmarks, native forms, audio/video, accessible tables) and modern CSS3 features (custom properties/variables, clamp(), calc(), modern viewport units dvh/svh, box-sizing, and CSS transitions).

faq.question: What is semantic HTML?
faq.answer: Semantic HTML means using HTML elements according to their intended meaning rather than their visual appearance. For example, using <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, and <footer> instead of generic <div> tags, and using <button> for clickable actions and <a> for navigation. This improves website accessibility for screen readers, strengthens technical SEO, and keeps code clean and maintainable.

faq.question: Will I learn Flexbox and CSS Grid?
faq.answer: Yes. Flexbox and CSS Grid are the core layout engines taught in this course. You will learn Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts (navbars, button groups, aligned rows) and CSS Grid for two-dimensional layouts (multi-column card galleries, responsive product grids, and complex page layouts).

faq.question: What is mobile-first responsive design?
faq.answer: Mobile-first responsive design is a professional methodology where you write CSS styles for small mobile screens first as the baseline layout, and then progressively introduce min-width media queries to enhance the layout for tablets, laptops, and wide desktop displays. This ensures fast mobile performance and clean layout adaptation.

faq.question: Does the course teach container queries?
faq.answer: Yes. The course introduces CSS container queries (@container) as a modern CSS capability. You will learn to set container-type: inline-size and write queries that adapt a component's layout based on the width of its parent container rather than only the entire browser viewport.

faq.question: Will I learn to build responsive navigation?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn to build responsive navigation structures that look clean on desktop screens and reflow gracefully on mobile devices, utilizing semantic <nav> landmarks, wrapping Flexbox patterns, and native <details>/<summary> disclosures without relying on fragile checkbox hacks.

faq.question: Will I learn HTML forms?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn to create accessible web forms using <form>, <label>, <input> types (text, email, tel, number, url, checkbox, radio), <select>, <textarea>, and <button>, along with native HTML5 validation attributes like required, pattern, and minlength.

faq.question: Do HTML forms automatically collect enquiries without a backend?
faq.answer: No. HTML forms provide the user interface and browser-side validation in static websites. However, receiving, storing, or emailing submitted user data requires an external form processing service (such as Formspree or Netlify Forms) or an authorized backend server. The course teaches this boundary clearly so you understand the difference between client-side interfaces and backend data processing.

faq.question: Will I learn CSS animations?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn performant CSS transitions (timing functions, durations, hover/focus micro-interactions) and subtle keyframe animations (@keyframes) using hardware-accelerated transform and opacity properties, along with the prefers-reduced-motion media query for accessibility.

faq.question: Does the course cover website accessibility?
faq.answer: Yes. Web accessibility (WCAG 2.2 Level AA awareness) is integrated throughout the curriculum, covering semantic HTML, landmark regions, logical heading hierarchies, descriptive link text, image alt text, and minimum color contrast ratios (4.5:1 for normal body text).

faq.question: Will I learn keyboard accessibility?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn to conduct manual keyboard audits using the Tab and Enter keys, verify logical DOM tab order, eliminate keyboard traps, and design visible, high-contrast focus rings using :focus-visible so keyboard users can navigate your websites effortlessly.

faq.question: Does it include Core Web Vitals and Lighthouse?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn current Google Core Web Vitals metrics—Largest Contentful Paint (LCP <= 2.5s), Interaction to Next Paint (INP <= 200ms), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS <= 0.1)—and run Google Lighthouse audits in Chrome DevTools to evaluate performance, accessibility, best practices, and SEO.

faq.question: Will I learn SEO basics?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn foundational technical and on-page SEO: crawlable HTML structures, optimized <title> tags (50–60 characters), <meta name="description"> (140–160 characters), canonical URLs, proper heading hierarchy, descriptive anchor text, and Open Graph social sharing tags.

faq.question: Will I learn Chrome DevTools?
faq.answer: Yes. Chrome DevTools is a primary tool in this course. You will learn to inspect the DOM tree, manipulate CSS styles live, examine the computed box model, test device widths in Device Mode, debug unexpected overflow, and check console and network logs.

faq.question: Does the course include Figma-to-code?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn Figma-to-code fundamentals: how to open a simple Figma design brief, inspect dimensions and spacing, extract color palettes and typography values, translate Figma Auto Layout frames into CSS Flexbox/Grid, and export optimized assets.

faq.question: Will I learn Git and GitHub?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn Git version control fundamentals (git init, git add, git commit, git status, git log), how to push repositories to GitHub, manage project files, and write professional README.md project documentation.

faq.question: Will I publish websites using GitHub Pages?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn how to configure GitHub Pages to publish your static website repositories to live public HTTPS URLs that anyone can access, verifying correct relative asset paths and live mobile behavior.

faq.question: How many website projects will I build?
faq.answer: You will build two complete, assessed portfolio website projects: a responsive commercial business landing page and a multi-page personal or professional portfolio website. Both are deployed live on GitHub Pages with complete source code.

faq.question: What is included in the portfolio?
faq.answer: Your portfolio includes two live published websites with public GitHub repositories, structured source code (HTML, CSS, images), responsive testing evidence across 5 viewports (320px to 1440px), manual keyboard accessibility checklists, W3C validation records, Lighthouse audit reports, and comprehensive README documentation.

faq.question: Will I learn JavaScript and React?
faq.answer: No. This course focuses exclusively on mastering HTML, CSS, responsive design, accessibility, and static site publishing. JavaScript application logic, DOM programming, and React component frameworks are specialized subjects taught in their own dedicated certification courses.

faq.question: Can I build a complete e-commerce application after this course?
faq.answer: You will be able to build beautiful, responsive e-commerce product landing pages, product card galleries, and shopping cart layouts using HTML and CSS. However, functional shopping cart logic, user accounts, databases, and payment gateway transactions require JavaScript and backend technologies covered in advanced courses.

faq.question: Does the course teach backend development?
faq.answer: No. Backend development (Node.js, Python, databases, APIs, authentication) is outside the scope of Course 55. This program is dedicated to static frontend website development with HTML and CSS.

faq.question: Will I receive editable source code?
faq.answer: Yes. You build all projects from scratch in your own Git repositories and retain complete ownership of all your HTML, CSS, asset, and documentation source files.

faq.question: Is this course a foundation for full-stack development?
faq.answer: Yes. HTML, CSS, and responsive design are the essential foundation of all web development. Whether you progress into JavaScript, React, frontend engineering, or full-stack web development, mastering clean HTML/CSS first makes learning advanced programming much smoother.

faq.question: Is this a government or Google certification?
faq.answer: No. This is an independent professional certification issued directly by Nova Skills Education Institute under ISO 9001:2015 educational standards. It includes a cryptographically verifiable QR code to validate your completed coursework and portfolio submissions. It is not an official endorsement from Google, GitHub, or any government body.

faq.question: What beginner-level career opportunities are possible?
faq.answer: Graduates can explore entry-level opportunities such as Junior Web Design Assistant, Entry-Level HTML/CSS Developer, Static Website Designer, Junior Frontend Production Assistant, Website Maintenance Assistant, Landing Page Specialist, or freelance static website creator for small businesses. Actual career outcomes depend on individual dedication, portfolio quality, and job market conditions; Nova Skills does not guarantee employment or salary outcomes.
